title: Where all beings have become the self, what delusion, what sorrow?
theme: For one who knows, when all beings have become the self, delusion and grief have no place.

words.role: sets the time or the place of the first clause; answered by tatra
words.context: Śaṅkara: «यस्मिन् काले यथोक्तात्मनि वा», ‘at which time, or in which self’; Deśika: «प्रणिधानसमये», ‘at the time of contemplation’; Madhva: «यस्मिन् परमात्मनि», ‘in which Supreme Self’

words.role: subject of abhūt (with ātmā as predicate)

words.gram: verb, root bhū (1st class, P.), root aorist 3rd sg. active
words.context: singular with a plural subject, agreeing with the predicate ātmā; see the morphology note

words.meaning: of [one] knowing, for one who knows
words.role: the person for whom the first clause holds
words.context: Śaṅkara: «परमार्थवस्तु विजानतः», ‘for one who knows the real’

words.meaning: of [one] seeing, for one who sees
words.role: the person for whom the questions are asked; parallel to vijānataḥ

sandhi.rule: The Upaniṣad witnesses leave final n unchanged before s. The Saṃhitā witnesses (K, M) write यस्मिन्त्सर्वाणि, with a t inserted between n and s, the insertion taught after ḍ by P. 8.3.29 (डः सि धुट्) and extended to n by P. 8.3.30 (नश्च). The words are the same.
i + ā → yā (P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि)); ā + e → ai (P. 6.1.88 (वृद्धिरेचि)); a + a → ā (P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः)); final t voiced to d before the voiced v (P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते)).

sandhi.type: visarga sandhi (-aḥ before a voiced consonant)
sandhi.rule: -aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes -o (P. 6.1.114 (हशि च), then P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः)).

sandhi.type: visarga sandhi (-aḥ before a vowel other than a)
sandhi.rule: -aḥ before a vowel other than a loses its visarga and the hiatus remains: the visarga becomes y (P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि)), which is dropped (P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)). Deśika’s mūla writes कश्शोक for कः शोक.

morphology.note: Root aorist of bhū: ‘has become’. The verb is singular though bhūtāni is plural; it agrees with the predicate ātmā (‘have become the self’), a construction Śaṅkara’s paraphrase keeps: «तान्येव भूतानि सर्वाणि परमार्थात्मदर्शनात् आत्मैवाभूत् आत्मैव संवृत्तः» — ‘those very beings have become, through the vision of the real self, nothing but the self’.

Genitive singular of the present participle of vi-jñā, ‘to know distinctly’. With anupaśyataḥ at the end of the verse it frames the mantra: ‘for the one who knows … for the one who sees oneness’. The genitive marks the person in whose experience the statement holds (‘for him’).
eka ‘one’ with the abstract suffix -tva: ‘one-ness’. The pada-pāṭha of VS 40.7 marks the suffix: «ए॒क॒त्वमित्ये॑क॒ऽत्वम्».

Locative of the relative pronoun, masculine or neuter. It can be taken as time (‘when’) or as place or person (‘in which self’, ‘in whom’); Śaṅkara gives both, and the other commentators choose one each (see Ambiguities).

anvaya: यस्मिन् विजानतः सर्वाणि भूतानि आत्मा एव अभूत् तत्र एकत्वम् अनुपश्यतः कः मोहः कः शोकः ।
syntax: A correlative sentence: yasmin … tatra, ‘in which … there’. The first half states a condition: all beings have become the self alone for the one who knows. The second half asks two rhetorical questions, ‘what delusion, what sorrow?’, meaning that there is none, for the one who sees oneness. The two genitive participles, vijānataḥ and anupaśyataḥ, refer to the same person.

ambiguities.topic: यस्मिन्: when, in which self, or in whom
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: «यस्मिन् काले यथोक्तात्मनि वा» (at which time, or in the self described); Deśika: at the time of meditation («प्रणिधानसमये»); Madhva: in the Supreme Self in whom all beings are («यस्मिन् परमात्मनि सर्वभूतानि»). The temporal reading makes the verse describe a moment of knowledge; the personal reading makes it describe the Lord.

ambiguities.topic: ‘All beings became the self’: identity or something else
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara reads a real identity seen by the knower. Deśika reads it as the Supreme Self being perceived as qualified by all things («परमात्मैव सर्वविशिष्टः प्रतीतः इत्यर्थः»), on the model of saying ‘I am a god’ of one embodied as a god, and rejects readings of sublation or identity of nature. Madhva construes differently: the Self in whom all beings are became present in all beings («स परमात्मैव तत्र सर्वभूतेष्वभूत्»).

Identity of all with the self (Śaṅkara: «आत्मैकत्वं विशुद्धं गगनोपमं»); the unity of the Lord qualified by all (Deśika: «सर्वविशिष्टैक्यमनुपश्यतः»), adding that ‘one’ here does not deny that anything else exists; or the one Lord in all beings (Madhva: «सर्वभूतेष्वेकत्वेन परमात्मानं विजानतः»).

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Counted as written, 15 and 16 syllables. As in mantra 6, the first half-line has 16 if the semivowel of bhūtāny ātmaiva is pronounced as a vowel (bhūtāni ātmaiva, as Advaita Sharada prints it), a resolution common in Vedic verse.

translation.literal: In which [state / self], for the one who knows, all beings have become the self alone — there, what delusion, what sorrow, for the one who sees oneness?
translation.readable: When, for one who knows, all beings have become the self, what delusion can there be, what grief, for one who sees the oneness?

beginner: This verse follows directly from the one before it. There, a person learned to see all beings in the self and the self in all beings. Here the verse takes one more step: for such a person, all beings have actually ‘become the self’. Then it asks two short questions — what confusion? what grief? — and leaves them unanswered, because the answer is obvious: none. Think about where grief and confusion come from. We grieve when we lose something separate from us that we needed, and we are confused when the world seems split into pieces that do not fit. If everything is seen as one, with nothing outside to lose and nothing that fails to fit, those two troubles lose their footing. The teachers who explained this verse disagree about what exactly ‘oneness’ means, as you will read below, but they agree on its fruit.
analogy: A wave that knows itself as the ocean does not mourn when it sinks back, nor wonder where it went: nothing has been lost from the water.

commentary.q: What does the mantra itself say?
commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The first half says that ‘in which’ — a time or a self — ‘all beings have become the self alone, for the one who knows’. The second half asks ‘there, what delusion, what sorrow, for the one who sees oneness?’, a rhetorical form that denies both. The mantra names two troubles, moha (delusion) and śoka (sorrow), and one cause of their absence, seeing oneness (ekatvam). It does not say what kind of oneness, and it does not say how the knower came to it; mantra 6 described the seeing that leads here.

commentary.q: Why does Śaṅkara say that saṃsāra itself is ended here?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara introduces the mantra as stating the same point as mantra 6 («इममेवार्थमन्योऽपि मन्त्र आह»). For him grief and delusion are the effects of not knowing, the seed of desire and action: «शोकश्च मोहश्च कामकर्मबीजमजानतो भवति, न त्वात्मैकत्वं विशुद्धं गगनोपमं पश्यतः» — they arise in one who does not know, not in one who sees the oneness of the self, pure and like the sky. Because the questions deny the very possibility of the effects of ignorance, he concludes that the whole of saṃsāra, with its cause, is uprooted: «सकारणस्य संसारस्यात्यन्तमेवोच्छेदः प्रदर्शितो भवति».

commentary.q: How can ‘all beings’ become ‘the self’ without ceasing to be?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Deśika answers by grammar. ‘All beings became the self’ is a statement of co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya), like calling an embodied person by the name of the body: the Supreme Self is perceived as qualified by all («परमात्मैव सर्वविशिष्टः प्रतीतः इत्यर्थः»). He explicitly rejects readings in which the world is sublated or the two are identical in nature («बाधोपचारस्वरूपैक्यादिपक्षाः बहिष्कार्याः»). The absence of grief follows because one who sees everything as the glory of another owns nothing; he quotes Janaka: «मिथिलायां प्रदीप्तायां न मे किञ्चित्प्रदह्यते» — ‘when Mithilā burns, nothing of mine burns’.

commentary.q: How is the second half built?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Two parallel genitive participles frame the verse: vijānataḥ ‘for one who knows’ closes the first line, anupaśyataḥ ‘for one who sees’ closes the second. The verb anupaśyati of mantra 6 returns as a participle, so that mantra 7 reads as the outcome of mantra 6. The questions use the masculine interrogative kaḥ twice, matching the masculine nouns moha and śoka. The Saṃhitā witnesses read यस्मिन्त्सर्वाणि, the Vedic junction with an inserted t; the words are unchanged.

commentary.q: Is this said of the liberated, or of the seeker?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Deśika raises the question himself: mantras 6 and 7 could be applied to the liberated, but, in keeping with what precedes, they are better taken as praise of the seeker: «एतौ च श्लोकौ यद्यपि मुक्तविषयतया नेतुं शक्यौ, तथाऽपि पूर्वानुगुण्यान्मुमुक्षुप्रशंसार्थत्वमुचितम्». For him ‘seeing’ here means knowledge born of scripture and the meditation rooted in it, and he says that this was established in the Śārīraka-bhāṣya (Rāmānuja’s Śrībhāṣya, as Deśika cites it): «मोक्षोपायोपदेशपरेषु सर्वेषु वाक्येषु दर्शनशब्द उपासनविषय इति शारीरकभाष्ये प्रत्यपादि». Śaṅkara, by contrast, speaks of the knower of the real.

advaita.text: The beings themselves, for one who knows the real, have become nothing but the self («आत्मैवाभूत् आत्मैव संवृत्तः परमार्थवस्तु विजानतः»). Oneness is identity; grief and delusion are products of ignorance, and with them saṃsāra and its cause end.

visistadvaita.text: Oneness is the unity of the Lord as qualified by all things («सर्वविशिष्टैक्यमनुपश्यतः»), not the denial of everything other than one: «न ह्ययमेकशब्द एकव्यतिरिक्ताभावपरः». The verse praises the seeker whose meditation sees everything as the body and glory of the Lord, and who therefore grieves over nothing as his own.

dvaita.text: The Supreme Self in whom all beings are is himself present in all beings; one who knows him as one in all beings has no delusion: «एवं सर्वभूतेष्वेकत्वेन परमात्मानं विजानतः को मोहः». Oneness is the oneness of the Lord everywhere, not identity of the self with the Lord. Madhva supports this with a verse he cites from a ‘Pippalāda recension’ (reported as cited, not verified).

schools.disagreement: Whether ekatva is the identity of self and all (Śaṅkara), the unity of the Lord with all as his qualifiers (Deśika), or the single Lord present everywhere (Madhva); and whether the verse describes the liberated knower (Śaṅkara’s emphasis) or the seeker in meditation (Deśika).

parallels.note: Yājñavalkya to Maitreyī: ‘where everything has become the self, then by what and whom should one see?’ The same words, sarvam ātmaivābhūt, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, where they lead to the question how there can be knowing of another at all.
Nārada has heard that ‘the knower of the self crosses grief’. The Chāndogya and the Īśā make the same connection between self-knowledge and the end of śoka.
‘Who sees the imperishable in the perishing, he sees.’ The Gītā ties right seeing to what does not perish among things that do, the ground on which grief at loss has no hold.

contemporary.text: Grief is not a mistake, and nothing in the mantra asks a mourner to stop mourning. What it offers is a diagnosis: sorrow takes hold where we experience the world as a set of separate things that can be taken from us. People who have sat with the dying sometimes describe a late, quiet shift — less clinging to what is ending, more sense of belonging to something that is not. The mantra names that shift as a way of seeing, ‘oneness’, rather than as resignation. Whether one reads oneness as identity or as the presence of one Lord in all, the point for an aging person is the same: what we are is not only what we are losing. This is a reflection on the teaching, not part of it.

reflect.beginner: Remember a time you were very sad about losing something. Was part of the sadness the feeling that it was separate from you and now gone?
reflect.deeper: If ‘oneness’ ends delusion and sorrow, is it the absence of others, or the presence of one in all others — and does the answer change what it would be like to lose someone?
reflect.practice: When a small loss happens today — a broken cup, a missed bus — pause and ask, ‘what of me is actually gone?’ Write down the answer in one line.

references.text: Mahīdhara (VS 40.7) follows Śaṅkara’s reading almost word for word and adds that the knower has reached it by reflecting on such sayings as «'आत्मैवेदम्' 'सर्वं खल्विदं ब्रह्मे'त्यादिवाक्य» (‘all this is the self’, ‘all this is Brahman’).
